installation.note: xz is part of xz-utils package, installed by default on Ubuntu and most Linux distributions

overview.summary: The xz command compresses and decompresses files using the LZMA2 compression algorithm, creating .xz files. It provides excellent compression ratios, often better than gzip or bzip2, making it popular for distributing software packages, kernel images, and archives. xz is also used by tar for creating compressed archives.
when_to_use: Compress files for storage or transfer

syntax.description: xz compresses files by default, creating .xz files and removing originals (unless -k is used). Use -d to decompress. Multiple files can be specified.

misconceptions.title: Deletes original by default
misconceptions.reality: xz removes original files after compression unless -k (keep) option is used
misconceptions.tip: Use -k option if you want to keep original files

misconceptions.title: Same as gzip
misconceptions.misconception: xz and gzip work the same way
misconceptions.reality: xz uses LZMA2 algorithm and typically provides better compression than gzip, but is slower
misconceptions.tip: Use xz for better compression, gzip for faster compression

common_pitfalls.description: xz removes original file after compression
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -k option to keep original files: 'xz -k file.txt'

common_pitfalls.description: xz can be slow, especially with high compression levels
common_pitfalls.solution: Use lower compression levels (-1 to -3) for faster compression, or use gzip for speed

common_pitfalls.description: xz can use significant memory, especially with high compression levels
common_pitfalls.solution: Use lower compression levels or ensure sufficient RAM available
Verify file is actually .xz format, or use 'file' command to check file type

related_commands.description: gzip is faster but provides less compression than xz
bzip2 provides good compression, between gzip and xz in terms of ratio and speed
tar -J creates tar archives compressed with xz
unxz is equivalent to 'xz -d' for decompression

best_practices: Use -k option to keep original files unless you're sure you don't need them
Use -9 for maximum compression when file size matters
Use -1 for faster compression when speed is important
Test compressed files with -t before distributing
Use -v to monitor progress for large files
Combine with tar for directory compression: 'tar -cJf archive.tar.xz directory/'
performance_tips: Lower compression levels (-1 to -3) are much faster with only slightly larger files
Use -T option to control thread usage on multi-core systems
xz is slower than gzip but provides better compression - choose based on priority
For very large files, consider using lower compression levels to save time

additional_notes.compression_ratio: xz typically provides 30-50% better compression than gzip
additional_notes.speed: xz is slower than gzip but faster than bzip2 for most files
additional_notes.tar_integration: Use 'tar -cJf' to create xz-compressed tar archives, 'tar -xJf' to extract
